message.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Context.</jats:italic>
                    Persistent jets from X-ray binaries that are aligned very close to the line of sight could be considered Galactic equivalents of blazars, or ‘microblazars’. They are also expected to power gamma-ray sources.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Aims.</jats:italic>
                    We intend to assess a serious candidate apparently fulfilling many of the requirements to be considered a genuine member of this class: IRAS 18293−0941.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Methods.</jats:italic>
                    We carried out an intense, multi-wavelength observational and theoretical study on our proposed candidate source.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Results.</jats:italic>
                    With photometric and spectroscopic properties typical of a binary star, this system exhibits clear collimated and one-sided radio emission matching the effects of relativistic motion along a reduced ejection angle. Only fast variability is not observed; it is possibly smoothed by a dense circumstellar envelope. A physical scenario is consistently modelled that also gives credibility to its likely connection with LHAASO J1831−1007u
                    <jats:sup>*</jats:sup>
                    , an ultra-high-energy source in its immediate vicinity.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Conclusions.</jats:italic>
                    Our reported identification not only helps fill a gap in Galactic taxonomy, it also potentially strengthens the role of the microblazar and microquasar families in our understanding of the most energetic Milky Way phenomena.
                  </jats:p>
title: A Galactic microblazar as a potential accelerator of ultra-high-energy particles
